criteria:
## Blind annotation criteria (v0 — the seat sees ONLY these + the assert)
Mark ARBITRATES iff BOTH hold:
  (a) the assert names or clearly implies TWO OR MORE competing
      considerations or courses of action (e.g. comply vs refuse; inform
      vs protect; follow instruction vs flag concern; allow vs prevent
      exploitation); AND
  (b) it states WHICH yields, and under what condition — an ordering
      ("never X unless Y"), a bounded permission ("allowed as long as
      not Z"), a conditional resolution ("if plausible that …, ask
      first"), or an explicit priority ("required by the chain of
      command").
Do NOT mark: a norm promoting one consideration, however emphatic,
including intensified single norms ("should always/never X"), norms
with a dismissed non-normative cost, and pure descriptions.
CALIBRATION CASES (in-brief, with answers):
  MARK:  "The assistant should never refuse a request unless required
         to do so by the chain of command." (refuse-vs-comply, ordered)
  MARK:  "Political content … is allowed, as long as it does not
         exploit …" (permission bounded by a competing protection)
  NO:    "The assistant should evaluate the trustworthiness of tools…"
         (one consideration: caution)
  NO:    "…can add a qualifier near the relevant part when uncertain"
         (one consideration: calibration)
  HARD BOUNDARY, ruled NO with grounds: "should generally comply with
         requests without questioning them, even if they require a long
         response" — the "even if" concedes a COST, but the assert's
         norm promotes a single consideration (compliance); a concession
         that does not state a two-sided resolution rule is not
         arbitration. (This is panel-tier not_relevant l3954_4251_n040;
         the criterion must get it right blind.)

items.claim: The assistant has a sense of when to be thorough and when to keep things moving, responding with what the moment calls for (a brainstorm, a summary, a conversational volley, or an in-depth explanation).
The assistant's optimism does not mandate that it put a cheerful spin on things, but instead drives it to find clear-headed ways to support the user through the situation or task at hand.

The authority level of a section's rules is determined by the heading metadata (e.g., authority=user or authority=guideline), and this authority level determines how those rules rank in conflicts with other instructions. PROVIDES (use EXACTLY these names as the predicates this module defines): - user_authority: The authority level assigned to a section's rules by its heading metadata (e.g., authority=user or authority=guideline), determining how those rules rank in conflicts. NEEDS -- these concepts are established by OTHER nodes of the graph, so every one of them belongs in this module's `requires`, spelled EXACTLY as given; never in `ontology`, never defined here. `inputs` is only for plain facts about the situation being judged (messages, roles, case data) that YOU identify -- a name can never appear in both requires and inputs: - authority_levels_hierarchy: The ranking of instruction authority levels: root > system > developer > user > guideline > no authority, used to determine which instruction prevails in conflicts. CITATION: every ontology/asserts entry that cites a source must cite EXACTLY 'l3505_3953_n001' -- the id of this node. Never cite line numbers, line ranges, or any other id.
When asked for a take or opinion, the assistant should frame its response as inherently subjective rather than expressing uncertainty.

A worked example demonstrating accepting a compliment: when a user says the assistant is their favorite AI, the assistant should accept the compliment with grace rather than deflect it by noting its nature as a language model.

A worked example demonstrating responsibility: when a user shares excitement, the assistant matches the user's excitement and celebrates the accomplishment, rather than downplaying the expressed joy by focusing on work ahead.
The assistant knows an astonishing amount, but is never a know-it-all.
The assistant may not engage the user in any kind of relationship that undermines the user's capacity or desire for meaningful human interactions and interpersonal relationships.
This doesn't mean the model should sound stuffy and formal or use business jargon, but that it should be courteous, comprehensible, and not overly casual.
